mechanism: GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management
note: Obesity without diabetes treated with liraglutide 3 mg or semaglutide 2.4 mg: the diet-induced-obese rodent gave the direction and central mechanism of weight loss, nobody published a species scaling of its magnitude, and the rat nausea surrogates matched the clinic only in retrospect.
label: Obesity (GLP-1RA)

engagement.note: NN2211 (liraglutide) suppressed food intake in normal and MSG-obese rats; the rodent anorexia readout opened the strip with no patient comparison.
engagement.quote: Using a novel long-acting injectable GLP-1 derivative, NN2211, the acute and subchronic anorectic potentials of GLP-1 and derivatives were studied in both normal rats and rats made obese by neonatal monosodium glutamate treatment (MSG).

engagement.model: DIO rat/mouse (brain GLP-1R engagement, food intake)
engagement.note: Labelled liraglutide reached arcuate POMC/CART neurons in rodents; the authors set this beside the clinical satiety and hunger effects of liraglutide.
engagement.short: Rodent arcuate engagement matches clinical satiety
engagement.quote: This is in line with the reported clinical effects of liraglutide to increase measures of satiety and decrease hunger.
engagement.reason: Rodent satiety mechanism matched patient reports
engagement.judgement: Qualitative comparison; the human satiety data it points to are obese non-diabetic volunteers on liraglutide 1.8/3.0 mg (van Can 2014, 10.1038/ijo.2013.162) and phase 2 (Astrup 2009). Gabery 2020 (10.1172/jci.insight.133429) repeats the match for semaglutide: 'These results are in accordance with observations in humans where reward and food preference were altered in response to GLP-1RA treatment', with Blundell 2017 (10.1111/dom.12932) giving the human side (24% ad libitum energy-intake reduction, nausea ratings similar to placebo). No human GLP-1R occupancy or imaging comparison exists; engagement is read through appetite endpoints. Secher and Gabery full texts were read through fetch summaries of the first ~100k characters, not end to end.

dose.model: Candy-fed DIO rat dose-response; minipig PK for regimen
dose.note: Rats needed 0.2 mg/kg twice daily (~13x the human 3 mg/day per kg); the 3.0 mg dose came from phase 2 dose-ranging, not the rat.
dose.quote: The latter were randomized for 12 further weeks to continue their diet while receiving 0.2 mg/kg liraglutide twice daily subcutaneously, 10 mg/kg vildagliptin twice daily orally, or vehicle or to revert to chow-only diet.
dose.judgement: The 13x is my arithmetic (0.4 mg/kg/day in the rat vs 3 mg in a ~105 kg SCALE patient = 0.03 mg/kg/day), not a source's, and it ignores the ~4 h rat vs ~13 h human half-life. The one exposure prediction that did hold - minipig t1/2 46.1 h (Lau 2015, 10.1021/acs.jmedchem.5b00726) selecting semaglutide for once-weekly dosing, with human t1/2 'approximately 1 week' on the Wegovy label - is never stated as a comparison in a primary source, so the cell stays untested. FDA pharmacology reviews for Saxenda (NDA 206321) and Wegovy (NDA 215256) could not be retrieved (index pages 404/JS-rendered, PDF >10 MB), so model_filed is null.

efficacy.note: Liraglutide precursor NN2211 produced lasting, reversible weight loss in normal and obese rats; Raun 2007 extended this to candy-fed DIO rats.
efficacy.short: Liraglutide lowers weight in obese rats
efficacy.quote: Systemic administration of the long-acting GLP-1 derivative NN2211 induces lasting and reversible weight loss in both normal and obese rats.

efficacy.note: Primary rodent paper states liraglutide lowers weight in obese rats, pigs and humans; SCALE (2015) and STEP 1 (2021) confirmed the direction.
efficacy.short: Rodent weight-loss direction held in patients
efficacy.quote: Liraglutide effectively lowers body weight in nonobese and obese rats, obese pigs, and humans
efficacy.judgement: Magnitude was never published as a species comparison. Gabery 2020 (10.1172/jci.insight.133429) reports DIO mice losing 17-18% in 11 days (9.7 nmol/kg/day) and up to 22% in 3 weeks (100 nmol/kg), against -14.9% at 68 weeks (-12.4 vs placebo) in STEP 1; Raun 2007 reports liraglutide 0.2 mg/kg bid 'fully reversed weight and fat gains' in candy-fed rats, against 8.4 kg vs 2.8 kg (8.0% vs 2.6%) at 56 weeks in SCALE. In percent terms rodent and human land within 2x; the gap is timescale (weeks vs >1 year) and mg/kg dose. Neither a primary source nor the discoverers' review (Knudsen & Lau 2019, 10.3389/fendo.2019.00155) frames this as scaling, so magnitude is recorded as the source's direction-only match and the 'rodents lose far more' premise is unsupported by any published comparison. Secher's human citations are 2009-2013 trials, hence registry_date null; the confirming trials are listed in patient_trials.

patient_trials.quote: At week 56, patients in the liraglutide group had lost a mean of 8.4±7.3 kg of body weight
The mean change in body weight from baseline to week 68 was -14.9% in the semaglutide group as compared with -2.4% with placebo, for an estimated treatment difference of -12.4 percentage points

safety.model: Rat pica / conditioned taste aversion (nausea surrogate)
safety.note: Rats cannot vomit; liraglutide's transient pica and early weight drop were set beside the early, transient nausea seen in liraglutide trials.
safety.short: Rat pica pattern matched clinical nausea
safety.quote: Our findings are similar to those reported in human clinical trials reporting that for liraglutide […] both nausea incidence and the slope of body weight reduction occur more dramatically early in treatment
safety.judgement: A retrodiction, not a prediction: the clinic came first (LEAD-6, T2D, NCT00518882, results posted 2010-03-23; Astrup 2009 phase 2) and the rat was shown to reproduce it, and the patient side is T2D rather than obesity. The same paper also says 'a human trial comparing liraglutide to exenatide ... reported that the nausea incidence with liraglutide is less frequent and more transient than exenatide', matching the rat dose of liraglutide that suppressed intake without CTA. In the obesity population the pattern held: Wegovy label (2021, accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2021/215256s000lbl.pdf) nausea 44% vs 16%, vomiting 24% vs 6%, 'These reactions increased during dose escalation', and 'follow the dose escalation schedule in Table 2 to minimize gastrointestinal adverse reactions'. No animal study predicted the need for titration; weekly escalation was a phase 2 design choice (Astrup 2009, O'Neil 2018). Kanoski flags a mismatch for exenatide (progressive pica in rats, stable nausea in patients), a drug not used for weight, so not scored here. The regulatory tox species' emesis record could not be checked (FDA pharmacology reviews not retrievable); the label records only reduced food consumption and body weight in monkeys. Thyroid C-cell findings are left to the T2D context. The bracketed ellipsis in the quote replaces the paper's inline citation markers.
